newsitem.title: USA: European, U.S. corporate chiefs prod governments.
newsitem.headline: European, U.S. corporate chiefs prod governments.

text.p: An influential group of European and American corporate chiefs meets this weekend in an effort to prod governments to move quickly on regulatory reforms that would lower the cost of transatlantic trade.

About 65 chief executive officers from large and small corporations gather in Chicago on Friday and Saturday to discuss ways to reduce duplication of regulation and certification so that businesses on both sides of the Atlantic can move products into each other markets faster and at lower costs.
The executives have become the most influential force in transatlantic trade relations since their first meeting in Seville, Spain, last year, said Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat.

"They are genuinely embedded into the transatlantic decision-making process in ways I would never have imagined when this was initiated a couple of years ago by (the late Commerce Secretary) Ron Brown," Eizenstat said.

"I have been in government on and off for 30 years and I have never seen a system in which the private sector was more effectively incorporated into the early stages of government decisions than this," he added.
The idea was for the business executives to tell their government leaders what initiatives they needed to lower trade barriers and reduce costs.
But some in the corporate world have expressed disappointment that government leaders have not moved more quickly on proposals to reduce regulatory duplication.

"I think it is fair to say that the business community on both sides of the Atlantic is disappointed with the results of the government's efforts so far," said Willard Workman, who heads the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's international division.

At issue is a number of so-called mutual recognition agreements in which the European Union and the United States would recognise each other's safety standards on certain products. The agreements are expected to save businesses millions of dollars in duplicative costs of certifying goods for each market.

"If it won't kill Americans, chances are it's not going to kill Europeans," said Frank Vargo, deputy assistant secretary for Europe at the U.S. Commerce Department, in explaining the concept behind the agreements.

Five mutual recognition agreements covering telecommunications equipment, electrical safety and electrical magnetic compatibility, pleasure crafts and veterinary medicine have been negotiated and are ready to be signed, U.S. officials said. The agreements involve about $40 billion in trade about evenly divided between the two sides, they said.

But they have been held up because of a dispute between the two trade partners over pharmaceuticals and medical equipment. European officials say the U.S. offer so far is inadequate and will not lower business costs, which is the objective. Europeans do not want to accept any of the agreements until the pharmaceutical and medical equipment issues are resolved.

Eizenstat said he expects the business leaders to do some prodding of government officials at the weekend meeting. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan are among the government officials expected to attend. Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky also may attend.
But European officials said they will "not be forced" to rush into agreements they are unwilling to accept.

"The business community will not consider what is on the table sufficient since it does not reduce the cost of doing business," European Commission Director-General of Industry Stefano Micossi said at a news conference in Washington.
"The fact that (the Chicago meeting) has come up is not a good reason to accept an insufficient proposal," he added.
